colonel.name: Colonel Rupert Whitby

fix: {count} {thing} at {scene}. Deal with them and I'll sleep soundly!
Some rotter has left {thing} all over {scene}. {count} of them, I counted. Sort it out, would you?
Standards, my dear photographer! {count} {thing} at {scene}, if you please.

The judges notice {thing}, you know. Deal with {count} of 'em anywhere you like.

thanks: Splendid! Absolutely first rate.
Jolly good show. The Committee thanks you.
Capital! I'll mention you in the minutes.
letters: My dear photographer, I've been chair of the Committee for eleven years and we have never placed higher than 'Commended'. With you here, I rather think this is our year.
I was in the Royal Engineers, you know. Bridges, mostly. Now I spend my days worrying about bunting. I find I don't mind a bit.
Mrs Whitby, God rest her, planted the daffodils on the Green. Every spring I count them. Four hundred and twelve this year.
Between ourselves, I've no idea what the judges look for. I simply imagine Mrs Whitby walking round with me and try not to disappoint her.
You've become part of the village, you know. Whatever the judges say, Honeycombe is prouder of itself than it has been in years. That's your doing.

postmistress.name: Mrs Edna Pemberton

fix: Between you and me, {scene} is a disgrace. {count} {thing}! Could you see to it, dear?
I've had three complaints this morning about {thing} at {scene}. {count} of them, apparently.
Your postcards sell ever so well, dear, but not with {thing} in them. {count} at {scene}, please.
fixAny: Could you deal with {count} {thing}, dear? Anywhere at all. I'll put the kettle on.

thanks: Oh, you are a dear. Thank you!
Lovely! I'll tell everyone it was you.
Marvellous. That'll give them something to talk about.
letters: Dear, I've run this Post Office for thirty-one years. I know everybody's business, but I keep it to myself. Mostly.
Your postcards go all over the country now. I had one returned from Dundee marked 'Too lovely to deliver'. Framed it, I did.
Mr Pemberton proposed to me at the kiosk, you know. He dropped the ring down the drain. We found it on the Tuesday.
Between ourselves, the Colonel is soft as butter. He brings me a bunch of the Green's daffodils every Easter and pretends they're from the Committee.
You're one of us now, dear. I've put your name on the parish Christmas card list. There's no going back.

stationmaster.name: Albert Figg

fix: Beg pardon, but there's {thing} at {scene}. {count} of them. The Great Western would be appalled.
Mr Figg reporting: {count} {thing} at {scene}. Not on my watch, if you'd be so kind.
Passengers deserve better than {thing}, I always say. {count} at {scene}, please.
fixAny: Keep the line tidy! {count} {thing}, wherever you spot them.

condition: I do like the Halt in {condition}. Would you take one for the waiting room?
combo: Like clockwork! Fix {count} in a row without stopping.

thanks: Right on time. Thank you kindly!
Shipshape and Bristol fashion!
Much obliged. The Great Western thanks you.
letters: Thirty-two years on the railway, and the Halt has won 'Best-Kept Station' four times. Five, if you count the year the judge fell asleep.
The milk train comes through at 6:12. I've never once seen it on time, and I've never once complained.
My late brother Harold drove the Cheltenham express. I still wave at every engine, just in case.
They say the branch line might close one day. I say: not while there's a flower bed on my platform.
I've put your photograph of the Halt up in the waiting room. Passengers ask who took it. I say, 'A friend of the line.'

landlady.name: Mabel Tuck

fix: Ooh, {scene} is in a state, love! {count} {thing}. Sort them and there's a pie in it for you.
My regulars have left {thing} all over {scene}. {count} of them. Honestly!
Be a treasure and deal with {count} {thing} at {scene}?
fixAny: Round the village, love! {count} {thing}, wherever you find them.

condition: The garden looks lovely in {condition}. Take one for the pub wall?
combo: Quick as a pint on a Saturday! {count} in a row, love.
nohint: Go on, no hints this time. I've got a shilling on you.

plays: {count} postcards of {scene}, love. The tourists buy them by the dozen.

thanks: You little treasure! Thanks, love.
Lovely! First half's on me.
Ha! Wait till I tell the regulars!
letters: The Bee & Bramble has been in my family since 1790. We've had highwaymen, a Prime Minister, and a very rude goose.
The secret to a good ploughman's is the pickle. The secret to the pickle is that I'll never tell you.
My Stan proposed to me in the snug. Mind you, he'd proposed to three others first. I was the only one who said yes.
The Reverend comes in every Thursday for 'parish business'. Parish business is my steak and kidney pie.
You've got a stool with your name on it now, love. Stan carved it himself. Don't look too closely at the spelling.

vicar.name: The Reverend Hollis

fix: Forgive me, but {scene} has {count} {thing}. Cleanliness is next to godliness, after all.
I've been praying about the {thing} at {scene}. {count} of them. Perhaps you are the answer?
Might I ask a small kindness? {count} {thing} at {scene}.
fixAny: Would you tend to {count} {thing}, wherever you find them? Bless you.

stamps: A postcard of {scene} for the parish magazine, three stamps if you can manage it.
condition: There's something heavenly about {condition}. Would you capture it for me?
combo: Swift as a bell-ringer! {count} in a row, if you please.
nohint: Have faith! Finish one scene without a hint.

collect: Keepsakes for the church bazaar! {count} would be wonderful.

thanks: Bless you! Truly.
Wonderful, simply wonderful. Thank you.
The bells shall ring for you! Well, at six o'clock anyway.
letters: I arrived in Honeycombe two years ago with a bicycle and a box of books. I'm told I'm still 'the new vicar'. I expect I will be for thirty years.
St Aldhelm's has eight bells and six bell-ringers. We make up the difference with enthusiasm.
Mabel's steak and kidney pie is the closest I have come to a religious experience outside the church. Please don't tell the Bishop.
I bicycle to the outlying farms every Wednesday. The hills are steep, but the views are a sermon in themselves.
Thank you for everything you've done. You've reminded us that caring for a place is a way of loving it.

combo: Busy as a bee! {count} in a row, dearie.

thanks: Oh, you are a honey. Thank you!
The bees are humming with joy!
Bless your heart. Have a jar of honey.
letters: I've kept bees at Rose Cottage for fifty-nine years. You must tell the bees everything, you know: births, marriages, and the cricket scores.
When my Walter died I told the bees first. They hummed all night. I like to think they were singing to him.
The secret to good honey is good neighbours. Clover in the fields, roses in the gardens, lime trees by the church.
I told the bees about you. They were very interested. They think you should settle down here.
When you go travelling, take a jar of my honey. A spoonful of Honeycombe, wherever you are.

thanks: Cheers! You're a star.
Brilliant! Right, I'm late.
Smashing. Tell Mrs Pemberton I was on time.
letters: I've been the postman here since I was seventeen. That's four years! I know every dog, gate and puddle in the parish.
I'm saving up for a motorbike. Mrs Pemberton says over her dead body. I think she's joking.
I'm sweet on Dot from the tea room. I've delivered her a card every day for a month. Haven't signed any of them yet.
I signed the card! She said yes to the pictures on Saturday! Don't tell Mrs Pemberton. She knows already, doesn't she.
When you go off to your next village, I'll deliver your letters myself. Even if it's Cornwall. Especially if it's Cornwall.
